text.tspan: Write — into the buffer, never to the server
(FUSE: write)
SetAttr — resize, set the mtime, or both
One intent, because the kernel sends them in one
callback and splitting them would mean chaining two
flows to answer it. Other attributes are no-ops
(FUSE: setattr)

g.text: ensure_scratch — make a writable buffer exist

text.tspan: Fail — a directory, or not writable
the mode we reported already said so
ensure_scratch
→ see below

g.text: FileIo seek(offset), write_all, read back the length

text.tspan: mark the buffer dirty
in-memory flag
DbWrite set_size
so the next getattr reflects the growth

g.text: truncate to zero, with no buffer open?

text.tspan: FileIo start from an empty buffer
No hydration: the base is about to be discarded,
so downloading it first would spend a full transfer
on bytes we throw away. This is the common overwrite
path — cp onto an existing file, every O_TRUNC editor.
The price: a later text merge has no base and falls
back to a conflicted copy
ensure_scratch
→ see below
remember it for the next upload
sent as X-OC-Mtime, so cp -p preserves timestamps.
Signed: a pre-epoch timestamp stays negative

g.text: done — back to the calling script

text.tspan: Net stream the full base into the buffer
Never capped, never held in RAM: editing a file
of any size must preserve all of it
FileIo seed the blob cache with that base
only with text merging on. Reads no longer populate
the cache, so without this a later 3-way merge finds
no base and degrades to a conflicted copy
register the buffer: clean, remembering the ETag
it was based on — the precondition a later
upload will assert
A write arriving during this hydration waits;
it must not abort it. The base is what a later
3-way merge is made of — and an editor autosaving
every two seconds would otherwise restart the
download forever, so it never finishes
